Cerebral Cortex: General Features

The cerebral cortex is the highest brain center, and its surface is greatly increased by sulci and fissures.

  • It is formed of two cerebral hemispheres separated by the longitudinal fissure.
  • The corpus callosum lies in the floor of the fissure and connects the two hemispheres.
  • It has 4 lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital.
  • Brodmann divided the cortex into 50 areas, numbered 1–50, on the basis of physiological studies.

Frontal Lobe

The frontal lobe contains area 4, area 6 and area 8.

Motor area 4 (primary motor area)

  • Site: precentral gyrus, anterior to the central sulcus.
  • It is highly excitable because it contains large pyramidal cells, the Betz cells.
  • Representation of the body: upside down (head below, lower limbs above), although the head itself is in the correct position (eyebrows up, chin down). It is crossed (the left area controls the right side) and depends on the activity of the muscle, not its size.

Layers and connections (6 vertical columns of cells)

  • Layers I & II: receive from non-specific thalamic nuclei.
  • Layers III & IV: receive from the premotor and sensory areas, PVNT, VLNT and area 4 of the opposite side.
  • Deep layers (V & VI): origin of the efferents. Betz cells of layer V give the pyramidal tracts; other efferents go to subcortical centers and the cerebellum.

Functions

  • Main origin of the pyramidal tracts.
  • Initiates fine, discrete voluntary movements.
  • Facilitates the stretch reflex and muscle tone.

Important notes

  • Area 4 shares in the extrapyramidal tract, so activating it after a pyramidal tract lesion still gives a response.
  • Muscles that act together, such as the respiratory muscles, are represented bilaterally in area 4 of both sides.
  • Area 4 represents movements, not isolated muscles: stimulating a site contracts whole flexors or extensors.
High-yield

Excitability of area 4 is increased by increased activity of other areas (sensory, visual, auditory) and by alkalosis. It is decreased by acidosis, hypoxia and the suppressor areas (4s, 8s).

Premotor area 6

  • Site: in front of area 4, separated from it by area 4s.
  • It contains no Betz cells, so it is less excitable than area 4.
  • Representation: inverted and crossed, but rougher than in area 4.

Functions

  • Main origin of the extrapyramidal tracts (with some pyramidal origin).
  • Initiates generalized, coordinated gross movements on the opposite side of the body.
  • Initiates subconscious associated movements, such as arm swinging during walking.
  • Helps area 4 perform and initiate isolated skilled voluntary movements.
  • Inhibits muscle tone, the stretch reflex and the grasp reflex.
  • Produces autonomic effects on heart rate and arterial blood pressure.

Area 8 (frontal eye field)

  • Site: posterior part of the middle frontal gyrus.
  • Causes conjugate deviation of both eyes to the opposite side.
  • Shares in the accommodation reflex to near vision.
  • Origin of the cortico-nuclear tract.

Parietal Lobe

Somatic sensory area I (areas 3, 1, 2)

  • Site: postcentral gyrus.
  • Representation: upside down and crossed. Large areas serve the lips, face and fingers (especially the thumb), according to tactile acuity and number of receptors. All sensations from any part of the body are represented.
  • Layers: I & II receive from non-specific thalamic nuclei; III is the interneuron layer; IV receives from different and fixed areas of the body; V & VI give efferents to the thalamus, brain stem and spinal cord.
  • Functions: receives impulses from PVNT; center for fine touch, proprioceptive sensation, vibration and fine gradations of temperature.

Somatic sensory area II

  • Site: upper wall of the lateral fissure, inferior to the postcentral gyrus.
  • Representation: less sharp than area I; face anteriorly, arm centrally, legs posteriorly.
  • Receives from both sides of the body, area I, and the visual and auditory areas.
  • Functions: cortical center of pain; role in sensory control of motor function.

Somatic association area (areas 5 & 7)

  • Site: parietal cortex behind sensory area I.
  • Receives from area I, PVNT, and the visual and auditory cortex.
  • Function: concerned with the meaning of sensory information (stereognosis).

Temporal and Occipital Lobes

Temporal lobe

  • Auditory sensory area (areas 41 & 42): hearing sensation from both sides.
  • Auditory psychic area (area 22): interpretation of auditory impulses.

Occipital lobe

  • Visual sensory area (area 17): the primary visual center.
  • Visual association area (areas 18 & 19): interpretation of visual impulses.

Parieto-temporo-occipital association area (area 37)

This is Wernicke’s area, at the supramarginal and angular gyri. It receives from the somatic association areas (5, 7), the visual interpretative areas (18, 19) and the auditory interpretative area (22), and interprets the different sensations.

It is more developed in the dominant hemisphere (the left in right-handed people) and is concerned with speech.

Clinical relevance

A lesion of Wernicke’s area causes failure to pick up the meaning of spoken and written words, with aphasia.

Speech

Speech is the highest function of the cerebral cortex and may take the form of written or spoken words.

Centers of speech (dominant hemisphere)

CenterSiteFunction
Visual speech center (sensory)Occipital lobe, areas 18 & 19Understanding written words
Auditory speech center (sensory)Temporal lobe, area 22Understanding spoken words
General interpretative area (Wernicke’s)Occipital lobe, area 37Connects sensory and motor speech centers; understands the meaning of words and begins the response
Broca’s area (motor)Face region in premotor area 6Essential for vocalization of speech
Exner’s area (motor)Hand region in premotor area 6Essential for expression of speech by writing

Act of speech

Spoken speech

  1. Perception

    Auditory sensory areas (41 & 42) perceive the spoken words.

  2. Word recognition

    Auditory association area (22) understands the words.

  3. Meaning

    Wernicke’s area understands the meaning and begins the response.

  4. Word production

    Impulses pass to Broca’s area to produce the words.

  5. Execution

    Face area of area 4, then the pyramidal tract to the cranial nerve nuclei, then the speech muscles (lips, tongue, larynx).

Written speech

Area 17
Areas 18, 19
Wernicke’s area
Exner’s area
Hand area of motor cortex
A.H.Cs of hand muscles

Area 17 perceives the written words and areas 18 & 19 understand them. Wernicke’s area gives full comprehension, Exner’s area passes the command to the hand area in the motor cortex, and the pyramidal and extrapyramidal tracts reach the A.H.Cs of the hand muscles, giving expression of speech by writing.

Check yourself

Which cells make area 4 highly excitable, and where is the area?

Large pyramidal (Betz) cells; the precentral gyrus, anterior to the central sulcus.

What happens to the eyes when area 8 is activated?

Conjugate deviation of both eyes to the opposite side.

Which speech center is essential for vocalization, and which for writing?

Broca’s area (face region of premotor area 6) for vocalization; Exner’s area (hand region of premotor area 6) for writing.

Key Points / Quick Review

Cortex overview

  • Four lobes; 50 Brodmann areas; hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum.

Area 4

  • Precentral gyrus; Betz cells; upside down and crossed; represents movements by activity.
  • Origin of the pyramidal tracts; facilitates tone and the stretch reflex.
  • Excitability falls with acidosis, hypoxia and suppressor areas.

Areas 6 and 8

  • Area 6: no Betz cells; main origin of extrapyramidal tracts; inhibits tone, stretch and grasp reflexes.
  • Contains Broca’s, eye movement, head rotation, skilled and Exner’s areas.
  • Area 8: conjugate deviation of the eyes to the opposite side; origin of the cortico-nuclear tract.

Parietal lobe

  • Area I (3, 1, 2): fine touch, proprioception, vibration, fine temperature.
  • Area II: cortical center of pain and sensory control of motor function.
  • Areas 5 & 7: meaning of sensory information (stereognosis).

Temporal and occipital lobes

  • 41 & 42: hearing; 22: auditory interpretation; 17: primary vision; 18 & 19: visual interpretation.
  • Wernicke’s area (37): supramarginal and angular gyri; lesion gives aphasia.

Speech

  • Spoken: 41/42, 22, Wernicke, Broca, area 4 face, cranial nerve nuclei, speech muscles.
  • Written: 17, 18/19, Wernicke, Exner, hand area, A.H.Cs, hand muscles.
